Issued at 258 AM EDT Fri Jul 24 2026

Mostly clear skies continue across the area today into this evening 
as weakening high pressure ridging retreats eastward as a low over 
northern Canada digs towards far northern Ontario. As the cold front 
of the low approaches the U.P. today and tonight, expect warm air 
advection to continue across the area, allowing high temperatures to 
get into the mid 70s to mid 80s this afternoon. With the weather 
being nice, today will be the best day to get any outdoor work done 
over the next few days as rain returns on Saturday...

The cold front descending from central Canada arrives early Saturday 
morning over the western U.P., moving over the central and eastern 
U.P. by the late morning to early afternoon hours. With the loss of 
LLJ support and the frontal boundary weakening as it continues to 
move southeastward with time, the severe weather chances are 
trending downward with the front's passage. Nevertheless, a stronger 
storm or two could be squeaked out as around 500-1000 J/kg of MUCAPE 
and 0-6 km bulk shear of 30 to 35 knots is expected ahead of an 
along the dying front. Looking at the latest CAMs, there is now a 
signal that some convection may pop-up behind the cold front later 
in the afternoon over mainly the central U.P.; should this more 
recent solution come into play, then it's possible we could see a 
small, slightly better severe weather threat mainly for hail and 
wind. SPC has accounted for the post-frontal convection in their 
latest Day 2 outlook by highlighting a Marginal Risk for severe 
weather over mainly the south central U.P. for marginally severe 
hail and wind (for late in the afternoon to early evening hours). 
Besides the severe chances (or lack thereof) for Saturday, expect 
rainfall amounts caused by the cold front's passage and the 
potential convection behind it to not be all that impressive; the 
latest REFS only a 10 to 30% chance for a wetting rainfall amount (a 
quarter inch or greater) for the central and east between 7 PM EDT 
today and 7 PM EDT Saturday. That being said, the chance is a little 
better over the eastern U.P., ranging anywhere from 30 to 75% 
depending on the location. 

While isolated showers and storms (25% or less chance) are possible 
Saturday night, chances increase once again come Sunday as a weak 
Clipper impulse skirts through the Upper Midwest/Upper Great Lakes. 
While we can certainly expect warmer temperatures and humid sfc 
conditions come Sunday (dewpoints may get to around 70F), the 
placement and track of the impulse hasn't been hammered out among 
the differing model suites yet given how weak it's predicted to be. 
Should the shortwave move through Wisconsin instead of the U.P. (or 
even along the Wisconsin/U.P. border), then Sunday may only have 
some lake breeze induced convection if anything at all. That being 
said, if the lake breeze or shortwave impulse is able to force 
anything up, there will be a some thick sfc-based CAPE to work with 
by the mid to late afternoon hours as well as abundant shear within 
the troposphere. Therefore, severe chances on Sunday remain low at 
this time as they will be highly dependent on the track of the 
Clipper impulse. 

A second and stronger Clipper low digs down into Lake Superior/the 
U.P. on Monday. Rain chances as well as rainfall amounts are greater 
with the passage of the Clipper on Monday; the latest NBM has 24-
hour rainfall amounts of greater than one quarter inch for Sunday 
night through Monday at 40 to 50% across the entire Upper Peninsula. 
Depending on the track of the Clipper, Monday could see the highest 
chances for severe weather, provided that the low goes through the 
U.P. or just north of the area and we are impacted by the warm 
sector; there could be 0-6 km bulk shear in excess of 50 kts and 
MUCAPE of around 1 to 2 kJ/kg. That being said, the chance for 
severe weather will be next to zero if the Clipper misses us to the 
south. So overall, while severe weather is possible with the Clipper 
come Monday (and chances may even be a little bit better), 
uncertainty on it remains high at this time given the model spread 
on the Clipper's track. 

As we get behind the Clipper and move into the middle of next week, 
expect high pressure to build over the central CONUS, traveling 
eastward and weakening with time as we head towards the end of the 
forecast period. This synoptic setup could bring us a positively-
tilted shortwave low or two from Canada during the middle-to-end of 
next week. Regardless, after a quick cooldown towards normal 
temperatures behind the Clipper, expect temperatures to 
progressively rise once again throughout most of the rest of the 
week as Gulf air advects back into the Upper Midwest.
